## INTRODUCTION AND SCOPE

This memorandum integrates the analyses of the four sub-questions arising from the research task: (1) whether a court or Crown Attorney has a duty to accommodate an accused's disability by communicating orally rather than in writing, and whether refusal constitutes discrimination; (2) whether courts and Crown Attorneys are subject to human rights legislation or enjoy immunity; (3) the range of monetary damages available for disability discrimination where accommodation was denied in court or government services; and (4) whether precedents exist in which an accused or litigant successfully claimed discrimination against a court or Crown for failure to accommodate communication needs.

Each sub-question has been examined within the strict citation constraints of this assignment. Only cases appearing in the "Top cases found" section have been cited. All pinpoint citations are copied from the provided "Pinpoint note" fields; no paragraph numbers have been invented. Where a legal principle could not be verified from the provided authorities, it is flagged as **[PRINCIPLE UNVERIFIED — requires further research]**.

**Bottom line:** On the authorities provided, the claim faces three formidable obstacles: (i) a threshold jurisdictional question about whether courts and Crown Attorneys are subject to the *Code* at all, which is unresolved; (ii) no provided precedent in which a litigant or accused *successfully* claimed discrimination against a court or Crown for failure to accommodate communication needs; and (iii) significant uncertainty in the quantum analysis, particularly regarding the statutory cap and its unit of application. The strongest analytical foundation is *Hughes v. Canada (Attorney General)*, [2016 FCA 271](https://canlii.ca/t/gvnp6), which recognized indirect discrimination where an employer insisted on a communication modality that disadvantaged a person by reason of disability despite an adequate alternative.

## LEGAL FRAMEWORK

### Statutory Regime

The primary governing statute is the *Human Rights Code*, R.S.O. 1990, c. H.19. Section 1 guarantees equal treatment in services without discrimination on the ground of disability. Section 5 prohibits discrimination in employment. Section 11 defines discrimination to include constructive (indirect) discrimination and imports the duty to accommodate to the point of undue hardship. Section 46.1 governs applications to the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario and its remedial powers.

The federal analogue is the *Canadian Human Rights Act*, R.S.C. 1985, c. H-6. Sections 7(b) and 53(2)(e)–53(3) are relevant: s. 7(b) prohibits adverse differentiation in employment on prohibited grounds, and ss. 53(2)(e) and 53(3) empower the Tribunal to award compensatory and additional damages respectively. Federal authorities are persuasive but not binding in Ontario.

### Constitutional Framework

The *Constitution Act, 1867* assigns criminal procedure to the federal government under s. 91(27) and the administration of justice in the province to the provinces under s. 92(14). Where human rights obligations are asserted against courts or Crown Attorneys in the exercise of their functions, the doctrines of federal paramountcy and interjurisdictional immunity may be engaged. Section 15 of the *Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms* provides a parallel but doctrinally distinct equality guarantee.

### Quasi-Constitutional Status of Human Rights Legislation

Human rights legislation is quasi-constitutional in character and applies unless there is a clear legislative pronouncement to the contrary: *Canada (House of Commons) v. Vaid*, [2002 FCA 473](https://canlii.ca/t/4hl0) at paras 64–65, 70.

## APPLICABLE LEGAL TESTS

The provided authorities disclose the following tests, which operate cumulatively.

### 1. Prima Facie Discrimination (Threshold)

A claimant must establish a distinction on a prohibited ground. The human rights test is less demanding than the *Charter* s. 15(1) test, requiring only proof of a distinction on a prohibited ground: *Canada (Human Rights Commission) v. Canada (Minister of National Revenue)*, 2003 FC 1280 at paras 8–10. The prohibited ground need only be a *contributing factor* to the adverse differentiation: *Clark v. Canada (Attorney General)*, 2007 FC 9 at paras 95–96.

### 2. Indirect Discrimination and Failure to Accommodate

An employer (or service provider) may commit indirect discrimination where it insists on a requirement that disadvantages a person due to disability, and refuses to consider an adequate alternative, unless it can justify the failure to accommodate. Once a prima facie case is made out, the burden shifts to the respondent to justify its conduct: *Hughes v. Canada (Attorney General)*, [2016 FCA 271](https://canlii.ca/t/gvnp6) at paras 2–5, 9–10.

### 3. Accommodation to the Point of Undue Hardship

The duty to accommodate requires reasonable adjustments up to the point of undue hardship, but does not require fundamental alteration of conditions where that would impose undue hardship: *Hydro-Québec v. Syndicat des employé-e-s de techniques professionnelles et de bureau*, [2008 SCC 43](https://canlii.ca/t/1zhnr) at paras 1, 3, 6.

### 4. Procedural Accommodation in the Justice System

Courts have an obligation to ensure litigants with disabilities can access a fair justice system, but granting specific procedural accommodations (including communication-format accommodations) is discretionary and assessed case by case: *Haynes v. Canada (Attorney General)*, [2023 FCA 158](https://canlii.ca/t/jz2c8) at paras 7–11. A fair trial claim based on a hearing or communication disability requires evidence that trial counsel objected or advised the court of the difficulty; the accused must demonstrate an actual inability to follow proceedings: *R. v. H.B.*, [2014 ONCA 334](https://canlii.ca/t/g6ndh) at paras 13, 15–16.

### 5. Testimonial Capacity

For testimonial capacity, s. 16 of the *Canada Evidence Act* requires a trial judge to assess the witness's *actual* ability to communicate and understand the oath rather than assume incapacity: *R. v. D.A.I.*, [2012 SCC 5](https://canlii.ca/t/fq0rb) at paras 101–104.

### 6. Immunity Framework

Where immunity is asserted against human rights legislation:
- **Stage 1 — Presumptive application:** Human rights legislation is quasi-constitutional and applies to all persons and institutions within its terms unless a clear legislative pronouncement excludes it. The party asserting immunity bears the burden: *Vaid*, [2002 FCA 473](https://canlii.ca/t/4hl0) at paras 64–65, 70.
- **Stage 2 — Constitutional immunity:** Where judicial functions are at issue, the question is whether the regime would require a judicial body to surrender a function that must be exercised exclusively by an independent judicial body, or would create a "shadow court" usurping superior court jurisdiction: *Cooper v. Canada (Human Rights Commission)*, [1996] 3 SCR 854 **[LEGACY CITATION — verify manually on CanLII]** at paras 10–13; *Reference re Code of Civil Procedure (Que.), art. 35*, [2021 SCC 27](https://canlii.ca/t/jgnxz) at paras 267, 272.

The immunity analysis is function-specific, not institution-wide. **[PRINCIPLE UNVERIFIED — requires further research]** as to whether Crown Attorneys enjoy any distinct immunity from human rights legislation.

### 7. Remedial Framework

Compensatory damages entitle the complainant to a "substantial award" for pain and suffering, and to compensation for lost wages and benefits where the evidence establishes loss: *Brown v. Canada (Royal Canadian Mounted Police)*, [2004 CHRT 24](https://canlii.ca/t/1hsg4) at paras 2, 3, 5, 7. Additional (aggravated) damages require conduct exceeding "stubbornness" — specifically, intention or recklessness: *Brown*, [2004 CHRT 24](https://canlii.ca/t/1hsg4) at paras 11, 14. Whether the statutory cap applies per complaint, per discriminatory practice, or per incident is unresolved: *Peters v. United Parcel Service Canada Ltd. and Gordon*, [2024 CHRT 140](https://canlii.ca/t/k99gl) at paras 45–48, 50–52.

## KEY CASES

### A. Duty to Accommodate / Discrimination

**Hughes v. Canada (Attorney General)**, [2016 FCA 271](https://canlii.ca/t/gvnp6) — The most factually analogous authority. The Tribunal found indirect discrimination where the employer insisted on verbal references despite the claimant's disability rendering them difficult, when written documentation was an adequate substitute (paras 2–5). The Federal Court of Appeal upheld the finding of prima facie discrimination where the employer refused to consider written documents after learning of the disability (paras 9–10). Establishes that requiring a particular communication modality, where an adequate alternative exists and the requirement disadvantages a person by reason of disability, may constitute discrimination absent justification.

**Hydro-Québec v. Syndicat des employé-e-s de techniques professionnelles et de bureau**, [2008 SCC 43](https://canlii.ca/t/1zhnr) — The Court addressed the interaction between the employer's duty to accommodate and the employee's duty to participate in the search for accommodation (para 1), described examples of adjusting working conditions (para 3), and identified conditions that may establish undue hardship (para 6). Confined to employment; does not address communication modality.

**Canada (Human Rights Commission) v. Canada (Minister of National Revenue)**, 2003 FC 1280 — Distinguished the *Charter* s. 15(1) test from the human rights test; the latter requires only a distinction on a prohibited ground (paras 8–10).

**Clark v. Canada (Attorney General)**, 2007 FC 9 — Sets out the s. 7(b) test (paras 95–96) and found the Commission erred in not referring a disability-accommodation complaint to the Tribunal (paras 97–100).

### B. Procedural Accommodation in the Justice System

**Haynes v. Canada (Attorney General)**, [2023 FCA 158](https://canlii.ca/t/jz2c8) — Acknowledged an obligation to ensure litigants with disabilities access a fair justice system (para 7) and considered a request for additional hearing time due to autism affecting information processing (paras 8–11). The Court held specific procedural accommodations are discretionary and assessed case by case. The appeal was dismissed; no accommodation failure was found (paras 81–82). Frames procedural accommodation as discretionary, potentially narrowing any asserted "duty" to communicate orally.

**R. v. H.B.**, [2014 ONCA 334](https://canlii.ca/t/g6ndh) — Acknowledged a duty to accommodate hearing problems in courts (para 13) but rejected the fair trial claim because trial counsel raised no objection and the court found the applicant heard and understood the proceedings (paras 15–16). The applicant's fresh audiologist evidence and specific instances of mishearing (paras 6–7) were insufficient absent a contemporaneous objection.

**R. v. D.A.I.**, [2012 SCC 5](https://canlii.ca/t/fq0rb) — Requires assessment of actual communicative ability under s. 16 rather than assumption of incapacity based on mental disability (paras 101–104).

**Eldridge v. British Columbia (Attorney General)**, [1997] 3 SCR 624 **[LEGACY CITATION — verify manually on CanLII]** — The *Charter* applies to delegated decision-makers exercising statutory authority; where their application of valid legislation infringes equality rights the appropriate remedy is under s. 24(1). No pinpoint paragraph is available. Addresses the *Charter*, not human rights legislation; does not address oral communication as an accommodation.

### C. Immunity of Courts and Crown Attorneys

**Canada (House of Commons) v. Vaid**, [2002 FCA 473](https://canlii.ca/t/4hl0) — Held that parliamentary privilege cannot be invoked to shield parliamentary employees from human rights legislation; the CHRA is quasi-constitutional (paras 64–65). For human rights legislation not to apply, there must be a clear legislative pronouncement to that effect (para 70). Neither parliamentary privilege nor PESRA precluded the application of the CHRA to employees of Parliament (para 111). The strongest authority against generalized institutional immunity.

**Cooper v. Canada (Human Rights Commission)**, [1996] 3 SCR 854 **[LEGACY CITATION — verify manually on CanLII]** — At paras 10–13, addressed the constitutional separation of powers and judicial independence, holding that certain functions must be exercised exclusively by independent judicial bodies. Authority for the proposition that the judiciary's institutional independence is constitutionally entrenched and cannot be displaced by ordinary legislation.

**Reference re Code of Civil Procedure (Que.), art. 35**, [2021 SCC 27](https://canlii.ca/t/jgnxz) — At para 267, recognized that s. 96 of the *Constitution Act, 1867* implicitly protects the historical jurisdiction of superior courts, the role of their judges, and the protection of the superior courts' independence. At para 272, described the purpose of the three-stage test as preventing legislatures from creating "shadow courts." Does not hold that courts or Crown attorneys are exempt from human rights legislation.

**Nelles v. Ontario**, [1989] 2 SCR 170 **[LEGACY CITATION — verify manually on CanLII]** — Held that the Attorney General and Crown Attorneys do not enjoy absolute immunity from civil liability for malicious prosecution. Concerns tort liability, not human rights legislation. **No paragraph numbers are available** for pinpoint citation.

**Commission des droits de la personne v. Attorney General of Canada**, [1982] 1 SCR 215 **[LEGACY CITATION — verify manually on CanLII]** — Addresses Crown privilege in the context of a human rights investigation. The excerpts do not directly address whether courts or Crown attorneys are subject to human rights legislation. **No paragraph numbers are available** for pinpoint citation.

### D. Monetary Damages

**Peters v. United Parcel Service Canada Ltd. and Gordon**, [2024 CHRT 140](https://canlii.ca/t/k99gl) — Frames the overarching question of maximum remedy under ss. 53(2)(e) and 53(3) CHRA at paras 45–48, and expressly observes at paras 50–52 that although many Tribunal decisions recite the existence of a $20,000 cap, they do not analyze whether it applies per complaint, per discriminatory practice, or per incident. The most directly relevant authority on the range-of-damages question.

**Brown v. Canada (Royal Canadian Mounted Police)**, [2004 CHRT 24](https://canlii.ca/t/1hsg4) — Confirms entitlement to a substantial compensatory award for pain and suffering; damages are remedial, not punitive; s. 53(3) requires intention or recklessness beyond stubbornness (paras 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 14).

**Canadian Human Rights Commission v. Canada (Attorney General)**, 2010 FC 1135 — Affirms lost income and benefits as a proper head of damages and confirms Tribunal discretion to calibrate pain and suffering awards to the evidence (paras 50, 74–75).

**Berberi v. Canadian Human Rights Tribunal**, 2011 FC 485 — Illustrates a concrete lower-end award — $4,000 for pain and suffering plus $5,814 in legal costs — and confirms that adequacy of the award is reviewable on judicial review (paras 2, 31).

**Walden et al. v. Canada (Social Development)**, [2008 CHRT 21](https://canlii.ca/t/1zf4n) — Confirms compensation for wage loss requires identification of an appropriate comparator group (paras 1, 8).

## ANALYSIS

### A. Whether a Duty to Accommodate by Oral Communication Exists

The provided authorities support the following propositions, with material qualifications.

**1. A duty to accommodate by alternative communication modality is recognized in principle.** *Hughes*, [2016 FCA 271](https://canlii.ca/t/gvnp6) at paras 2–5, 9–10 is directly instructive on the structure of the analysis: where a decision-maker insists on a communication format that disadvantages a person by reason of disability, and an adequate alternative exists, the refusal to adopt the alternative may constitute indirect discrimination. Although *Hughes* concerned verbal references rather than oral versus written communication, the reasoning applies by analogy to a requirement that an accused communicate in writing where a disability impairs that modality.

**2. The duty is bounded by undue hardship and reasonableness.** *Hydro-Québec*, [2008 SCC 43](https://canlii.ca/t/1zhnr) at paras 1, 3, 6 confirms that accommodation is required only to the point of undue hardship and need not fundamentally alter conditions. Whether communicating orally rather than in writing would impose undue hardship on a court or Crown Attorney is a fact-specific inquiry not resolved by the authorities provided.

**3. Procedural accommodation in the justice system is discretionary.** *Haynes*, [2023 FCA 158](https://canlii.ca/t/jz2c8) at paras 8–11 is the only provided case addressing accommodation within the justice system itself. It characterizes the granting of specific procedural accommodations as discretionary and case-by-case. This suggests a court retains latitude to decline a particular modality request, which may narrow the practical force of any asserted "duty" to communicate orally.

**4. The evidentiary hurdle is high.** *H.B.*, [2014 ONCA 334](https://canlii.ca/t/g6ndh) at paras 15–16 requires evidence that trial counsel objected or advised the court of the difficulty, and an actual inability to follow proceedings. On the facts as described, the accused did request oral communication, which may satisfy the "objection or request" component — but the *H.B.* standard also requires demonstrating actual inability to follow proceedings, which the accused's difficulty with reading and writing may or may not meet on the evidence.

### B. Whether Courts and Crown Attorneys Are Subject to Human Rights Legislation

This is the threshold jurisdictional question and it is **not resolved** by the provided authorities.

**Courts as Respondents.** The strongest constitutional argument for judicial immunity derives from *Cooper*, [1996] 3 SCR 854 **[LEGACY CITATION — verify manually on CanLII]** at paras 10–13 and *Reference re Code of Civil Procedure (Que.), art. 35*, [2021 SCC 27](https://canlii.ca/t/jgnxz) at paras 267, 272. These establish that judicial independence and the core jurisdiction of superior courts are constitutionally protected. If a human rights tribunal were to assume jurisdiction over the *adjudicative functions* of a court — for example, by reviewing judicial conduct or ordering a court to decide a matter in a particular way — that would raise serious s. 96 and separation-of-powers concerns.

However, the immunity principle is **function-specific, not institution-wide**. The provided authorities do not support the proposition that a court, qua employer or qua service provider, is wholly exempt from human rights legislation. *Vaid*, [2002 FCA 473](https://canlii.ca/t/4hl0) at paras 64–65, 70 militates against broad institutional immunity: human rights legislation is quasi-constitutional and applies absent a clear legislative pronouncement to the contrary. No such clear pronouncement appears in the Ontario *Human Rights Code* provisions identified.

**Crown Attorneys.** Crown attorneys exercise prosecutorial discretion, which is constitutionally protected to some degree. *Nelles*, [1989] 2 SCR 170 **[LEGACY CITATION — verify manually on CanLII]** establishes that prosecutorial immunity from tort liability is not absolute. By extension, a claim of absolute immunity from human rights legislation would be difficult to sustain. However, *Nelles* addresses tort liability, not human rights legislation, and **no paragraph numbers are available** to support a more precise analogy. The more relevant framework is *Vaid*, [2002 FCA 473](https://canlii.ca/t/4hl0) at para 70: absent a clear legislative pronouncement excluding Crown attorneys from the *Code*, the Code applies. The manner in which it applies remains unsettled.

**Crown Immunity and Division of Powers.** The provided authorities do not establish a general Crown immunity from human rights legislation. *Commission des droits de la personne*, [1982] 1 SCR 215 **[LEGACY CITATION — verify manually on CanLII]** addresses Crown privilege in the investigative context but does not resolve the immunity question, and **no paragraph numbers are available**. The division-of-powers dimension is engaged but not resolved: ss. 91(27) and 92(14) create potential federal-provincial tension, and the doctrines of interjurisdictional immunity and federal paramountcy may be relevant, but none of the provided cases applies these doctrines to the question at hand. **[PRINCIPLE UNVERIFIED — requires further research]**.

### C. Whether Refusal Constitutes Discrimination

The provided cases confirm the discrimination test is less demanding than under the *Charter* (*Canada (Human Rights Commission)*, 2003 FC 1280 at paras 8–10) and that refusal to accommodate an adequate alternative can constitute indirect discrimination (*Hughes*, [2016 FCA 271](https://canlii.ca/t/gvnp6) at paras 9–10). However, no provided case applies this to oral versus written communication by a court or Crown Attorney, and no provided case addresses the defences (bona fide justification, undue hardship) in that specific context. The determination will turn on whether oral communication is an "adequate alternative," whether the failure to adopt it disadvantages the accused by reason of disability, and whether the court or Crown can justify its refusal by reference to undue hardship.

### D. Monetary Damages

The provided authorities establish the structure but do not yield a reliable range for the specific fact pattern (accommodation denied in court or government services).

**Compensatory awards are fact-and-evidence driven.** The Tribunal has discretion to calibrate pain and suffering and wage-loss awards to the record: *Canadian Human Rights Commission*, 2010 FC 1135 at paras 74–75; *Walden*, [2008 CHRT 21](https://canlii.ca/t/1zf4n) at para 8. No numeric range for denial-of-accommodation-in-services is articulated in the materials.

**The cap is the live controversy.** *Peters*, [2024 CHRT 140](https://canlii.ca/t/k99gl) at paras 50–52 makes clear that the per-complaint/per-practice/per-incident question is analytically unresolved. If the cap is per discriminatory practice, an accommodation denial involving multiple discrete practices could plausibly exceed $20,000. This is a 2024 decision and therefore reflects the current state of the question, but the Tribunal in *Peters* frames it as a question rather than a settled rule.

**Aggravated damages are available but bounded.** The threshold in *Brown*, [2004 CHRT 24](https://canlii.ca/t/1hsg4) at paras 11, 14 is meaningful: a denial of accommodation grounded in bureaucratic inertia or repeated refusal after notice may support a finding of recklessness, but "stubbornness" alone will not. On these materials, a well-documented denial after a clear accommodation request is more likely to satisfy the s. 53(3) threshold than a single isolated oversight.

**The low end is real.** *Berberi*, 2011 FC 485 at para 2 demonstrates that awards can be modest ($4,000 pain and suffering) even where discrimination is found. Counsel should not assume high quantum from liability alone.

**Constitutional overlay is unaddressed.** No provided case engages paramountcy or interjurisdictional immunity as it affects remedial quantum or Tribunal jurisdiction over court/Crown-attorney services. **[PRINCIPLE UNVERIFIED — requires further research]**.

### E. Precedents Involving Successful Claims Against Courts or Crowns

The sub-question asks specifically for precedents where a claimant *successfully* claimed discrimination against a court or Crown for failure to accommodate communication needs. On the cases provided, **no such precedent exists.**

- *H.B.*, [2014 ONCA 334](https://canlii.ca/t/g6ndh) at paras 15–16 — fair trial claim rejected.
- *Haynes*, [2023 FCA 158](https://canlii.ca/t/jz2c8) at paras 81–82 — appeal dismissed; no accommodation failure found.
- *D.A.I.*, [2012 SCC 5](https://canlii.ca/t/fq0rb) at paras 101–104 — accommodation principle articulated, but no discrimination claim against a court or Crown.

Query: ("monetary damages" OR compensation OR award) /p ("disability discrimination" OR "failure to accommodate") AND ("human rights" /p damages) AND (range OR quantum OR "amount awarded")
Note: Yielded a useful cross-section of tribunal and court awards for disability discrimination, including cases where accommodation was denied in the provision of services. Provided a workable range of damages and the factors tribunals consider in fixing quantum.
Cases selected:
- Peters v. United Parcel Service Canada Ltd. and Gordon, 2024 CHRT 140
- Brown v. Canada (Royal Canadian Mounted Police), 2004 CHRT 24
- Canadian Human Rights Commission v. Canada (Attorney General), 2010 FC 1135

SEARCH 4
Query: (accused OR litigant OR claimant) /p disability AND ("failure to accommodate" OR "denied accommodation") AND (court OR Crown OR "Crown Attorney") AND ("human rights" /p discrimination) AND (communication /p (oral OR written))
Note: Returned a small number of matters in which an accused or self-represented litigant with a disability alleged discrimination arising from the manner in which a court or the Crown communicated with them. The Ontario Court of Appeal decision and the Federal Court decisions were the closest factual analogues.
Cases selected:
- R. v. H.B., 2014 ONCA 334
- Hughes v. Canada (Attorney General), 2016 FCA 271
- Clark v. Canada (Attorney General), 2007 FC 9
